messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Thomas, a 19-year-old counselor of European descent, has been struggling with the aftermath of a life-threatening illness that he encountered just over a year ago. His journey since then has been marked by a series of intense triggers and maladaptive strategies that have profoundly impacted his daily life. The traumatic event began when Thomas was rushed to the hospital after collapsing at work. The stark white walls, antiseptic smell, and medical equipment surrounding him during the emergency procedures were seared into his memory. Since then, any visual or olfactory cue reminiscent of the hospital has triggered intense reactions. Medical equipment such as needles and drips, undergoing a medical examination, or even the faint scent of antiseptics can send Thomas spiraling back to that terrifying moment. These triggers have led Thomas to adopt several maladaptive strategies. He avoids thinking about anything discussed in therapy sessions because it reminds him of his time in the hospital and the fear he felt then. Instead of facing these memories, he chooses to stay up until very late, delaying sleep as a way to avoid confronting the intrusive thoughts that come with it. His aversion extends beyond mere avoidance; Thomas actively steers clear of hospitals, ambulances, and any physical examinations. Thomas’s triggers not only lead to maladaptive strategies but also exacerbate his feelings of threat. Unexpected movements around him can startle him, causing a reaction as if he were still in danger. When something reminds him of the stressful experience, he experiences strong physical reactions such as rapid heartbeat and sweating. These heightened states of alertness make it difficult for him to feel safe or relaxed. These threats have further reinforced his maladaptive strategies. The fear of encountering medical cues keeps him up late into the night, where he finds a temporary respite from the intrusive memories that plague him during the day. However, this avoidance has only deepened his sense of threat, creating a vicious cycle where his fears and reactions intensify over time. The trauma has also led Thomas to develop negative appraisals about himself and his body. He feels like nothing in his life holds any meaning anymore, a sentiment that stems from the overwhelming fear and uncertainty he experienced during his illness. This loss of meaning is intertwined with his belief that his body can no longer be trusted. His physical reactions, such as heart palpitations or nausea, remind him that his body is not reliable and often feels like an enemy. These negative appraisals have fueled Thomas’s maladaptive strategies further. The feeling that nothing in his life holds meaning anymore has driven him to avoid situations where he might face reminders of his illness, including therapy sessions. He is certain that talking about it will only deepen the sense of futility and fear. Additionally, this belief that his body is unreliable and an enemy contributes to his heightened startle response and physical reactivity. The cycle of triggers, maladaptive strategies, threat perceptions, and negative appraisals has become tightly interwoven in Thomas’s life. His job as a counselor, which once gave him purpose and meaning, now feels meaningless because it often involves discussing difficult topics that remind him of his traumatic experience. This occupational stress has strained both his work relationships and personal life with his girlfriend. What finally brought Thomas to seek help was the realization that he could no longer function normally without these overwhelming fears and reactions. He is most afraid that his body will betray him again, but he is also hopeful that therapy can provide a way out of this cycle of fear and avoidance. His greatest hope is to regain a sense of trust in himself and find meaning in life once more. Thomas’s journey underscores the complex interplay between triggers, maladaptive strategies, threat perceptions, and negative appraisals that characterize his struggle with PTSD. As he begins therapy, it is clear that breaking this cycle will require addressing each component to help him reclaim a sense of safety and purpose in his life.
